# How Cáishén got its accent back

The ASCII form *caishen* is missing something. **Cáishén** restores the ​marks the source language used to distinguish this name from a thousand others — and those marks change how the name is read, pronounced, and understood. This post explains, with the full ‌scholarly record behind it, what each restored mark preserves: the Chinese characters evidence, the reconstructed sound, the myths the name carries, and the mechanical logic of what each restored mark preserves. By ‌the end, the marks in Cáishén will look less like ornaments and more like what they are — recovered evidence, pinned back in its proper place.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Cáishén
- ​**ASCII form:** caishen
- **Meaning:** "God of wealth"
- **Domain of influence:** Wealth, Prosperity, New Year
- **Pantheon:** Chinese
- **Restoration:** Preserves stress
- **Original script:** 財神 (Chinese characters)
- **Live domain:** cáishén.com

## Overview

**Cáishén** (*caishen*) — Wealth, Prosperity, ​New Year · God of wealth — belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Wealth, Prosperity, New Year". The name means "God of wealth".

**Cáishén** belongs to ​the Chinese tradition, where it is associated with wealth, prosperity, new year.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Cáishén** and serves its temple at [caishen.com](https://punicodex.com/caishen/). The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature ​— a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists. The plain ASCII form *caishen* survives as a modern convenience imposed ​by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Chinese characters as **財神**. Etymologically it means ‌"God of wealth".

Cái (財) 'wealth, riches'; Shén (神) 'god, spirit' — the popular deity of prosperity worshipped at New Year.

The ASCII form *caishen* survives only because the early domain-name system ​could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Cáishén** recovers the stress accent of the original directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves ​at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **c** → **C** ‌— Same, capitalized
- **a** → **á** — Acute tone mark
- **i** → **i** — Same
- **s** → **s** — Same
- **h** → **h** — Same
- **e** → **é** — Acute tone mark
- ​**n** → **n** — Same

The canonical temple for this name is served at **caishen.com**.

## Etymology & Roots

The recorded derivation reads: Cái (財) 'wealth, riches'; Shén (神) 'god, spirit' — the ‌popular deity of prosperity worshipped at New Year.

The root gloss is "wealth god."

The reconstruction is classed as attested.

## The Original Script

The name is written in Chinese characters as **財神**. ​This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *caishen* and the PuniCodex restoration **Cáishén** are measured: the restoration preserves its pitch accent of the written form, so that a reader ‌typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/caishen/** — Chinese Reconstruction.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **C** — Initial character of the restored form ​Cáishén.
- **áishén** — Remainder of the name, preserving the distinctive marks of the Chinese tradition.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'CAISHEN' — pronounce the restored form with attention to ​the preserved diacritics and length.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Chinese** — Cáishén, the restored Unicode form of the name

Cáishén preserves both features because the Chinese form preserves distinctive ​features that ASCII loses: stress, length, or special characters.

## Mythology

The stories of **Cáishén** circulate within the Chinese corpus, where the figure embodies wealth, prosperity, new year.

### Primary Attestation (Sources)

Cáishén is attested ​in the canonical Chinese sources as a figure associated with wealth, prosperity, new year.

### Name and Meaning (Etymology)

The name means "God of wealth" and reflects the figure's role in the tradition. ​**Cáishén** is the Chinese god of wealth, appearing in several forms including Zhào Gōngmíng, Bǐ Gān, and Fàn Lí. He confers prosperity on families and businesses during the Lunar New Year, when ‌images of him are displayed and burned as offerings. His cult reflects the moral ambiguity of wealth: it must be attracted ethically and shared generously. Merchants place his image beside cash registers ​and householders burn paper effigies to ensure his favor in the coming year.

### One Office, Many Gods (The Title)

The two characters 財神 simply mean **'god of wealth'** — a title, not a ‌personal name, and the tradition treats it that way. There is no canonical birth-story of Cáishén; instead, the office has been filled, again and again, by figures the culture wished to honor: ​a loyal minister, a canonized marshal, an honest merchant, even the red-faced war-god Guan Yu in some regions. The clearest early attestations belong to the **Song dynasty** (960–1279), when China's commercial revolution ‌made wealth a god worth petitioning; the Ming-era compendium *Santjiao soushen daquan* and the novel *Fengshen Yanyi* then fixed the cast of avatars. The sources disagree openly about who 'really' holds the ​office — which is the honest thing for a god of fortune, since every trade, region, and dynasty wants to claim him. A god with many faces is a god owned by many ‌classes; Cáishén's multiplicity is the theology of a civilization that decided prosperity itself was divine.

### Zhao Gongming on the Black Tiger (The Marshal)

The fullest avatar-story comes from the Ming novel *Fengshen ​Yanyi* (**Investiture of the Gods**). During the fall of the Shang dynasty, **Zhao Gongming**, a hermit of Mount Emei, comes down to aid the doomed house with his black tiger, his iron ‌whip, and his magic pearls; battle after battle turns on his power, until Jiang Ziya's side breaks him with Lu Ya's sorcery — an effigy of straw pierced by arrows. When the ​war ends and the fallen are canonized, Jiang Ziya invests the dead marshal as the **God of Wealth**, true lord of the dragon-tiger altar, mounted on his tiger, whip in hand, gold ingot ​ready — with four assistant deities who manage the welcoming of treasure, the gathering of valuables, the inviting of wealth, and the profiting of markets. The novel turns fortune into a **bureaucracy**: ‌wealth flows not from luck but from an office, staffed, audited, and answerable — a very Chinese answer to the oldest of prayers.

### Bi Gan's Missing Heart (The Heartless Minister)

The civil ‌face of the god descends from an atrocity recorded by **Sima Qian** in the *Shiji* (c. 90 BCE, 'Basic Annals of Yin'). **Bi Gan**, uncle and chief minister of King Zhou of Shang, ‌remonstrated against the tyrant's cruelties until the king, goaded on by his favorite Daji, ordered the minister's heart cut out — to test the old claim that a sage's heart has seven ​openings. Because Bi Gan died **heartless**, later tradition reasoned, he is beyond greed: no bribe reaches a god who has no heart to desire one. He became the **Civil God of Wealth**, ​the form merchants and bankers trust, usually shown in an official's robes holding a ruyi scepter and a scroll. The logic is ruthless and perfectly practical: the only trustworthy custodian of wealth ‌is the man whose desire for it has been surgically removed — a parable about greed built on a mutilation, and one of the darkest etiologies any god carries.

## Symbols & Iconography

The ​iconography associated with Cáishén concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Restored Name** — The Unicode form Cáishén carries the original marks of the ​Chinese tradition.
- **Source Script** — Attested in the original script as 財神.
- **Domain** — Wealth, Prosperity, New Year
- **Etymology** — God of wealth

- **The gold ingot (yuanbao)** — The boat-shaped silver-gold ingot ‌held by every avatar of Cáishén — wealth made visible and graspable.
- **The black tiger** — Marshal Zhao's mount; the tiger that can carry wealth away as easily as it brings it.
- ​**The iron whip** — Zhao Gongming's weapon, disciplining the pursuit of riches — wealth taken unjustly is wealth reclaimed.
- **The ruyi scepter** — 'As you wish' — the wish-granting wand of the Civil ​God of Wealth.
- **The account book** — The ledger in which the god's office records each household's fortune for the coming year.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material record for Cáishén survives in ‌a small number of securely identified remains, catalogued below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

Cáishén is attested in the textual ​and iconographic record of the Chinese tradition.

## Realm & Domain

**Cáishén** belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is associated with wealth, prosperity, new year.

### Wealth

The central domain of Cáishén in ‌the chinese tradition.

### God of wealth

The name signifies "God of wealth".

### Unicode Restoration

The restoration Cáishén recovers what plain ASCII caishen flattens.

### Original Attestation

Attested in the sources as 財神.  Devotees also ​associate him with gambling windfalls, business negotiations, and the honest accumulation of family prosperity.

### Marshal Zhao

Zhao Gongming: black tiger, iron whip, gold ingot — the Martial God of Wealth canonized in ​the Fengshen Yanyi.

### The Civil God

Bi Gan, the Shang minister whose heart King Zhou cut out; without a heart, he cannot be greedy, so merchants trust him.

### Welcoming the God

On ​the fifth day of the New Year, businesses reopen with firecrackers to be first to receive him.

### The Five Paths

Worshipped in sets of five — the Five Gods of Wealth, bringing ​fortune from every direction of the compass.

## Across Cultures

Cáishén appears within the Chinese tradition and has influenced later retellings, artistic depictions, and scholarly study. The Unicode restoration preserves the name's distinctive orthography ‌for contemporary use.

Within the Chinese tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[bagua|Bāguà]], [[change|Cháng'é]], [[fuxi|Fúxī]], [[guandi|Guāndì]], [[guanyin|Guānyīn]], and [[houyi|Hòuyì]].

## Cultural Legacy

Cáishén continues to appear in scholarship, art, and popular ‌reception as a significant figure of the Chinese tradition. Restoring the name in Unicode returns the original marks that ASCII removes. Cáishén remains one of the most commonly invoked deities in Chinese ​popular religion, especially during New Year observances.

## A Meditation

Cáishén embodies wealth, prosperity, new year in the Chinese imagination. The name's restoration is not merely cosmetic: it recovers the stress, length, and script that make ​the figure recognizable in the source tradition.

## The Unicode Restoration

Cáishén preserves stress. The ASCII fallback *caishen* still resolves everywhere, but it is the restored form that carries the name's full information. ‌Across the 7 characters of the name, the restoration adjusts 2: 2 marks of stress (á, é). That is the whole thesis of this temple: the marks are the message.

## The Domain Name

The restored name is live as a working domain: **cáishén.com**, ‌which the DNS carries in punycode form as xn--cishn-xqa3d.com — an ASCII-compatible encoding that lets a non-ASCII name travel the global network without breaking older infrastructure. The visitor sees Cáishén; the machines ​see the encoding. That duality is the engineering compromise on which the entire restoration rests, and it is why a name written the way its own tradition wrote it in Chinese characters can ‌now be typed into any browser on earth.

## Why This Restoration Matters

The marks in **Cáishén** were never lost; they were only waiting ​for a carrier that could hold them. Now that the carrier exists, the burden flips: every use of *caishen* is a choice to leave evidence on the table. The PuniCodex temple keeps ​the restored form in circulation — as a domain, a dataset entry, and a scholarly argument — so that the choice to use it stays easy. Accent by accent, macron by macron, that ‌is how the original names come back: not with a single grand gesture, but with a spelling that finally works everywhere.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name ​is a small map. In **Cáishén**, the journey from the ASCII fallback *caishen* to the Unicode form can be read letter by letter, and each letter tells a story. Of the 7 characters, ‌5 remain unchanged; they anchor the name to its modern shape. The remaining adjustments recover marks the source tradition used to distinguish this name from every other word built from the same ​letters.

The **c** stays as it is — Same, capitalized.

The **a** becomes **á** — Acute tone mark.

The **i** stays as it is — Same.

The **s** stays as it is ‌— Same.

The **h** stays as it is — Same.

The **e** becomes **é** — Acute tone mark.

The **n** stays as it is — Same.

Together these changes are not decoration. They ‌are the minimum set of marks needed to keep the name legible in its own tradition. Remove them and you still have a string of letters; you no longer have the name ​as it was written.

## Cáishén in Its Tradition

**Cáishén** does not stand alone. It belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is counted among 59 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. Its sphere ​— Wealth, Prosperity, New Year — places it beside other figures who govern similar aspects of experience. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way of ​keeping the name in the company of its kin. When the address bar shows **Cáishén**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living catalog of ​myth. That catalog is the point of the project. Every restored name is a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, between a tradition ‌and a trend. **Cáishén** is one such vote.
